en: In the *Laghvamoghānandinī Śikṣā*, it should be understood that the word "ja" occurs at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), at the beginning of a word (*pada*), and in the case of conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) and elided vowels (*avagraha*); that which is final is traditionally known as "ya. (1)
In the same way, with a concentrated mind, one should likewise perceive the other [element] through its corresponding subtle form; and following the fourth [element],
one should abide in the state at the beginning of words and even where there is no interruption, as well as at the end of a conjunction.
Excluding the two *rahu*s, that which is slightly touched is desired for the *yāna*s.
One should know the *iṣyamitra*s; just as there may be *rocana* for the mouth, so too should one purify the *sūrya*, while others are deluded like a heap. 3–4.
When a prefix is seen even at the beginning of a word,
it should be understood as slightly separated [from the following word] by means of a pause (padaccheda);
furthermore, the letter *ya* may optionally be inserted, and it is always present in the case of a reduplicated form (*āmreḍita*).

"Wherever... there," "may he sacrifice," and likewise from the word "thus" (tathā); 6. Now, therefore, that which follows is "the higher," and likewise from the word "not" (na) following [the word] "thus"; these also occur in the preceding [section], and so too from the word "thus. 7.

Now, we shall illustrate those [cases] where the *v* following the prefix *ava*—whether it occurs at the beginning of a word or elsewhere—is light when followed by a consonant (*yatpara*) and not otherwise. In the recitation (*pāṭha*), [the forms] *vo*, *vā*, *vāi*, *vi*, and *vau* [are examples]. When following a prefix (*upasarga*), the *v* is light.
Now, let it not be that [the rule] "vibhāṣā amreḍite yvoḥ" applies to sounds;
whatever characteristic belongs to one [consonant], let that also belong to the letter *v*.
Wherever there might be a distinction, that shall now be explained.

If *vo* or *vām* are used as indeclinables (*nipāta*) expressing the sense of "you," and if the substitutes (*ādeśa*) have the meaning of "optionality" (*vikalpa*), they are remembered as being slightly articulated (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).
For example: *devīvaḥ savitā*, *yā vām*, *vāto vā*, and likewise *iti na tat*.
In that regard, "vāyu," "ṛtaspate," and "tān" are proclaimed [as instances where] the *samprasāraṇa* occurs as formulated by the author of the Sūtra;
this should be understood to apply to all Vedic branches (*śākhā*) except for those of the Vājasaneyins.
Even when there is a contradiction regarding the phonetic characteristics, if identity of recitation is observed,
it should be understood accordingly, as in the case of "yajñā yajñā va" (RV 8.61.14). Furthermore,
the anusvāra should have a duration of two mātrās when followed by an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant.
Whether from a short or a long [vowel], from the hearts of the gods—15.
You are the uniter, O Lioness; in a conjunction, a short [vowel] is desired;
"śrathāya" is the middle [term]; the conjunction is not repeated twice—16.

Having understood the destruction of the Veda, a wise man should certainly not speak [of it] improperly; rather, having summoned him to a secluded place, he should speak correctly, for in this way his dharma is not lost. 17.
Thus ends the *Śrīlaghvamoghānandinī-śikṣā*.
